newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin warns officials to answer for actions.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin warns officials to answer for actions.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, holding his first official meeting since his heart surgery two weeks ago, told Russian officials on Tuesday to get ready to answer for their actions during his absence from the Kremlin.

During the more than 90-minute meeting with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin at Moscow's Central Clinical Hospital, the 65-year-old president also discussed the growing tension in neighbouring Belarus and expressed his alarm.

Yeltsin's warning to Kremlin and government officials that he is investigating how they have performed during his absence signalled his intention to get tough in response to the power struggles that have erupted since he has been away.

"After (Yeltsin's) return to the Kremlin representatives of the executive branch of power at all levels will have to answer for decisions they made, for their consequences and for their mistakes," Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said.
"It is completely natural that the president should take stock of things before his return."
Yastrzhembsky, who described the talks as Yeltsin's first working meeting, although he has had shorter discussions, said the process had already begun. He gave no details.
The spokesman made clear the Kremlin administration and the government were being reviewed, but did not say if any officials would be sacked or name those who were under the microscope.

The opposition communists have accused Kremlin chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais of usurping power in Yeltsin's absence and of engineering the dismissal on October 17 of the ambitious national security adviser, Alexander Lebed.

Other officials were involved in intense jostling for position before Yeltsin's operation on November 5 in the belief that the president might not be well enough to undergo surgery and that a presidential election could be called early.

Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin was likely to be moved later this week from the Central Clinic Hospital to the Barvikha sanatorium on the outskirts of Moscow. Doctors have said he will spend about a month there before returning to the Kremlin.

Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin had issued a series of orders to Chernomyrdin showing his concern about non-payment of pensions, a struggle with parliament over the 1997 budget and the need to start talks on reconciliation with the opposition.
He did not say when Yeltsin would make an address to the nation, which the Kremlin had initially suggested might take place last week. He gave no reason for the apparent delay.

Russian television has still shown no new footage of Yeltsin since the operation, although the liberal newspaper Sevodnya published a photograph of the president smiling with his granddaughter and his wife Naina at the weekend.

Yeltsin and Chernomyrdin expressed their alarm at the situation in Belarus, where President Alexander Lukashenko and parliament are locked in a struggle over his plans to hold a referendum on Sunday on increasing his powers.

"The president and the prime minister expressed alarm about rising tension in Belarus society and the hope that common sense and the art of political compromise will replace the ambitions and confrontations among politicians," Yastrzhembsky said.
Moscow has been moving slowly towards closer integration with Belarus, a former Soviet republic on Russia's western border, and appears embarrassed and worried by the stand-off.
Chernomyrdin and Yeltsin discussed the situation in rebel Chechnya. Chernomyrdin did not say when he would go ahead with a planned visit to Chechnya, saying more preparation was needed.

The prime minister informed Yeltsin about his trip to the southern Dagestan region this weekend after an explosion tore apart a block of flats there. Flags were flying at half-mast across Russia in honour of the 68 people killed in the blast.
